site.title: TEMPO: Semantic-Action Decoupled RL Post-Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
site.subtitle: A two-timescale reinforcement learning framework that adapts semantic projection and robot action generation at different update frequencies.
site.meta_description: TEMPO is a semantic-action decoupled reinforcement learning framework for post-training vision-language-action models with separate semantic and action update frequencies.

summary.title: Why TEMPO changes the update clock

cards.title: Module-aware RL
cards.body: The semantic projection layer and action expert are optimized through dedicated TD3-style loops instead of one composite policy update.

cards.title: Different update frequencies
cards.body: The semantic projection changes conservatively, while the action expert receives more frequent updates from online control feedback.

cards.title: Long-horizon improvement
cards.body: TEMPO reaches 81.7% SR5 and a 4.59 average completed-chain length on CALVIN, with gains that grow along the instruction chain.

sections.title: One pretrained policy, two adaptation needs
paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning gives a VLA policy a useful starting point, but it does not optimize closed-loop success under the states created by the policy's own actions. Online reinforcement learning can supply that feedback, yet a uniform policy update treats every trainable component as if it should adapt at the same pace.

TEMPO starts from a functional asymmetry. The semantic projection layer sits close to the pretrained semantic space, so rapid changes can shift the latent action seen by downstream control. The action expert is directly exposed to target-task dynamics and execution error, so it can benefit from denser control-side updates.

sections.title: Separate the learning loops, then set their clocks
sections.section_note: A shared robot rollout feeds two representation-specific TD3 loops, each with its own replay buffer, twin critics, targets, and optimizer.

figure.alt: Full TEMPO framework with a frozen VLM, slow semantic projection loop, fast action expert loop, replay buffers, critics, and environment feedback.
figure.caption: The semantic loop operates in the h-to-z space; the action loop operates in the z-to-action-chunk space. Both are driven by the same environment reward.

equation.label: Policy decomposition
equation.body: The frozen VLM produces h_t, the semantic projection produces latent action z_t, and the action expert produces action chunk a_t.

cards.title: Preserve pretrained semantics
cards.body: The vision-language backbone remains frozen throughout RL post-training.

cards.title: Slow semantic adaptation

cards.body: A separate action critic updates the action expert in the (z_t, a_t) control space.

cards.title: SR5 over FLOWER
cards.body: TEMPO raises SR5 from 77.8% to 81.7% after RL post-training.

cards.title: SR5 over DeFI
cards.body: TEMPO also exceeds the strongest non-RL baseline reported in the table.

paragraphs: TEMPO ranks first across SR1-SR5 and Avg. Len. in the reported CALVIN comparison. Relative to its FLOWER initialization, the gain grows from 0.6 points at SR1 to 3.9 points at SR5, while the SR1-to-SR5 drop narrows from 21.6 to 18.3 points.

FLOWER-RL improves SR5 only to 78.4% when the projection layer and action expert are updated together as a composite actor. The result supports the paper's central claim: allocating updates by module role matters in addition to applying RL itself.

sections.title: The gain depends on both modules and the ratio
paragraphs: Updating either module alone improves over the pretrained FLOWER reference, but neither single-module variant reaches the full method. The frequency study further separates the effect of RL from the effect of update allocation: equal-frequency 1:1 updating remains near the reference, while 5:1 and 10:1 produce clear long-horizon gains.

The best tested setting is 5:1, where the action expert receives five updates for every semantic projection update. This gives the control module more opportunities to absorb interaction feedback while the latent-action interface changes more conservatively.
